## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter the reader should be able
to:

- Explain why a continuous-integration service, by
  rebuilding a compendium on a machine that carries
  none of the author's undeclared state, catches the
  'works on my machine' failure at its source.
- Name the three automated gates a
  continuous-integration workflow runs on every change,
  state what each one proves, and make each one fail
  once on purpose.
- Distinguish verification (level L3) from the capture
  levels below it, and explain why verification compares
  computational outputs with a committed baseline, within
  a stated tolerance, rather than the rendered report.
- Read and adapt a checksum manifest that guards the
  integrity of raw input data.
- Describe how a continuous-integration workflow adapts
  to the research archetype, so that a package, a
  manuscript, and a simulation each run the gates
  appropriate to them.
- Relate automated in-house checking to independent
  external verification schemes such as CODECHECK and
  artifact badging.

## Orientation

Consider a registry study whose analysis is finished,
whose manuscript is written, and whose lockfile and
container recipe are committed to version control. The
author has done, to all appearances, everything this
book has asked. The packages are pinned (@sec-dependencies),
the environment is fixed in an image (@sec-containers),
the report is literate and regenerates its own figures
(@sec-literate). The compendium sits, by the author's
account, at level L2, a pinned environment. But how
does the author know that the captured environment
actually rebuilds, on a machine that is not the one
where the work was done? The honest answer, until
something tests it, is that the author does not know.
A lockfile can reference a package version that has
been pulled from its repository. A Dockerfile can
depend on a base image whose digest has drifted. A
script can quietly rely on a file that lives only in
the author's home directory and was never committed.
None of these announce themselves on the machine where
the work already runs, because on that machine the
missing piece is present.

This chapter is about the instrument that closes the
gap between a reproducibility claim and its
demonstration. Continuous integration, which we shall
abbreviate CI, is a service that rebuilds the
compendium from its committed inputs on every change.
It works in a fresh environment that carries none of
the developer's accumulated and undeclared state, and
runs a battery of checks against the result. We shall see
that CI captures no new layer of the determinant stack.
Its whole contribution is to *validate* that the layers
already captured actually suffice, which is a different
and complementary act. The distinction between
capturing reproducibility and validating it, drawn in
@sec-intro and carried through every chapter, reaches
its operational form here: pinning is capture, and CI,
together with the verification command it runs, is
validation.

We then take the ladder to its top rung. Verification,
the L2-to-L3 transition, does not capture more; it
confirms what has been captured by regenerating the
computational outputs and comparing them, number for
number and within a stated tolerance, against a
recorded baseline.
The subtlety, which we shall press, is in what gets
compared: a derived dataset, a fitted model object, a
results table, and emphatically not the rendered PDF or
HTML, whose bytes carry timestamps and font identifiers
that defeat a naive comparison. We close with the
schemes by which reproducibility is checked from
outside the author's own project entirely, during peer
review.

## The analyst's contribution

Continuous integration is highly automated, and it is
tempting to regard it as a matter of copying a workflow
file into a repository and forgetting it. That view
mistakes the machinery for the judgment. Three
decisions remain the analyst's, and no tool makes them.

1. **The analyst decides what counts as a correct
   output, and records the baseline.** Verification can
   compare a regenerated result against a recorded one,
   but it cannot know which results matter or what
   tolerance is acceptable. Whether the baseline is a
   derived dataset, a coefficient table, or a single
   summary statistic, and whether an agreement to the
   last bit or to a stated numerical tolerance is
   required, is a scientific choice the analyst must
   make and defend.

2. **The analyst decides which gates the compendium's
   archetype warrants.** A CI workflow can run `R CMD
   check`, a render gate, and a dependency-manifest gate,
   but not every archetype needs all three. An R-package
   archetype has no report to render; a simulation
   archetype may run a reduced pipeline under CI and the
   full one elsewhere. Matching the gates to the
   archetype, so that CI tests what actually needs
   testing without imposing a render gate on a project
   that has nothing to render, is the analyst's call.

3. **The analyst reads a CI failure as evidence, not as
   an obstacle.** A red build is CI doing its job: it
   has found, on a clean machine, a dependency the
   author's machine supplied silently. The discipline
   is to treat the failure as a true report about the
   compendium's reproducibility rather than as a
   nuisance to be suppressed, and to fix the captured
   inputs rather than the check.

::: {.callout-note}
## The vocabulary of this chapter

- **Continuous integration (CI).** A hosted service that,
  on every committed change to a repository, checks out
  the code onto a fresh virtual machine, rebuilds the
  project, and runs a defined set of checks, reporting
  success or failure automatically.
- **Workflow.** The file, written in YAML, that tells the
  CI service what to do: which events trigger it, what
  environment to run in, and what commands to execute. On
  GitHub these files live under `.github/workflows/`; on
  GitLab the single file is `.gitlab-ci.yml`.
- **Runner.** The fresh, ephemeral machine (usually a
  virtual machine or a container) on which the CI service
  executes the workflow. It is discarded after the run,
  so nothing persists between runs except what the
  workflow explicitly restores.
- **`R CMD check`.** R's own quality gate for a package,
  which among many checks verifies that every dependency
  declared in `DESCRIPTION` is installed and findable. A
  research compendium built as an R package inherits this
  gate for free, for its package skin only: `analysis/`
  is excluded from the build and never checked.
- **Render gate.** A CI check that re-renders the
  compendium's report (an R Markdown or Quarto document)
  from source and fails the build if the render errors.
- **Dependency-manifest gate.** A CI check that enforces
  the dependency invariant of @sec-dependencies. In its
  strict, R-package form it requires every package the code
  uses to be declared in `DESCRIPTION` and pinned in
  `renv.lock`. For a research compendium, whose
  `DESCRIPTION` declares only the API exported from `R/`
  while analysis scripts legitimately draw on packages
  present in `renv.lock` but not in `DESCRIPTION`, it
  enforces the weaker inclusion that every package the code
  uses is pinned in `renv.lock`.
- **Verification.** The act of rebuilding the compendium's
  environment from its recipe, re-running the analysis in
  it, and comparing the regenerated computational outputs
  with a committed baseline, within a stated tolerance, by
  means of a baseline test (@sec-testing); passing it is
  what the ladder calls level L3.
- **Checksum.** A short fingerprint, computed from a
  file's or an object's bytes by a hash function such as
  SHA-256, with the property that any change to the input,
  however small, changes the fingerprint. A stored
  checksum lets a later run detect that an input has been
  altered.
- **Forge.** The platform that hosts the repository and
  runs its CI, such as GitHub or GitLab. The forge governs
  where the code lives and which CI dialect the workflow
  is written in; it pins nothing about the computational
  environment.
:::

## The machine that is not yours

We begin with the single idea from which everything in
this chapter follows. The reason an analysis reproduces
on the machine where it was written is, in part, that
the machine is generous: it supplies, without being
asked, a package installed months ago and never
recorded, a system library that some other project
needed, a data file sitting in a home directory, an
environment variable set once in a shell profile. Every
one of these is undeclared state, and every one of them
is invisible precisely because it is present. The
'works on my machine' failure is not a lie; it is a
true report about a machine that happens to carry more
than the compendium declares.

Continuous integration removes the generosity. When a
change is pushed, the CI service provisions a fresh
runner, a virtual machine or container that has just
been created and carries nothing but a clean operating
system. It checks out exactly what is under version
control, no more, and attempts to rebuild the
compendium from those committed inputs alone. If the
analysis depended on anything the author never declared,
the rebuild fails, and it fails here rather than in a
reviewer's hands or a colleague's re-analysis a year on.
The CI machine catches the 'works on my machine' failure
at its source for a reason that is almost tautological:
the CI machine is, by construction, not yours. It cannot
supply your undeclared state because it does not have it.

It is worth being precise about what this does and does
not add. Continuous integration captures no new layer of
the determinant stack. It does not pin a package version,
fix an operating system, or record a session option;
those are the work of the lockfile and the container,
done before CI runs. What CI adds is the repeated,
adversarial test that the capture already performed is
sufficient. A captured-but-never-retested compendium
suffers a slow decay, the failure mode in which a
declared environment quietly stops rebuilding as its
external references drift, and no one notices because no
one has tried to rebuild it. CI is the standing test
that would notice. Removing CI from a repository lowers
no level on the ladder; the compendium is exactly as
reconstructable as before. It simply stops being
checked, and becomes trusted rather than tested.

## What the checks are: the three gates

A CI run on a research compendium executes, in the
general case, three gates. We take them in turn, because
the division of labor among them is exact.

The first is **`R CMD check`**. Because a research
compendium is structured as an R package (@sec-compendium),
it inherits R's own quality gate at no additional cost.
Among its many checks, the one that matters most for
reproducibility is early and simple: it verifies that
every package the code in `R/` uses is declared in
`DESCRIPTION`, and that every declared package is
installed and findable. On a fresh runner this is a real
test, because the runner has only what the lockfile
declared.

Its scope is exact, and narrower than it looks. The check
runs on the package that `R CMD build` makes, and a
compendium's `.Rbuildignore` excludes `analysis/`, so the
analysis scripts are never parsed, never run, and never
scanned for packages (@sec-compendium). `R CMD check`
validates the package skin, `R/`, the tests, and
`DESCRIPTION`, and nothing else. Within that scope there
is a second trap: an undeclared package used in `R/` is
reported as a WARNING, not an ERROR, so the gate fails on
it only if it is told to fail on warnings. A workflow that
passes `error_on = "error"` to `rcmdcheck`, as many
hand-written workflows do, lets the undeclared dependency
through with a green build.

The second is the **render gate**. Where the compendium
carries a report, an R Markdown or Quarto document that
regenerates its own figures and tables, the workflow
re-renders it from source on the runner. A render that
errors, because a chunk references an object that no
longer exists or a package that was not restored, fails
the build. Of the three gates it is the one that executes
the analysis code: a report that sources the scripts under
`analysis/`, or calls the functions they define, runs them
on the runner, against the restored library and nothing
else. The render gate is the literate document's
validation counterpart: @sec-literate seals the prose to
the code, and the render gate confirms, on a clean
machine, that the seal holds. It needs the data on the
runner. The cohort this book uses is synthetic and
committed for that reason; where the real data are
restricted, CI renders against a synthetic stand-in and
the real render runs inside the environment approved for
the data. Committing the data to turn a red render gate
green is never the fix.

The third is the **dependency-manifest gate**, the
automated form of the dependency invariant developed in
@sec-dependencies. In its strict form, appropriate to the
R-package archetype, the invariant is a double inclusion:
the set of packages the code actually uses must be a
subset of the set declared in `DESCRIPTION`, which must in
turn be a subset of the set pinned in `renv.lock`. A
research compendium is looser, because its `DESCRIPTION`
declares only the API exported from `R/` while its
analysis scripts legitimately use packages that appear in
`renv.lock` but never in `DESCRIPTION`. For a compendium
the operative invariant is therefore the single inclusion
that every package the code uses is pinned in `renv.lock`,
and the strict `DESCRIPTION`-inclusion gate does not apply.
The gate scans the source, `analysis/` included, for
`library()`, `require()`, and `pkg::fun()` calls, reads
`DESCRIPTION` and `renv.lock`, and stops with an error if
a used package is not pinned. Because it reads the analysis
scripts, it is the gate that covers what `R CMD check`
cannot see. Its core needs no special tool; `renv` itself
can find the packages the code uses:

```r
# ci/dependency-gate.R
used <- unique(renv::dependencies('analysis')$Package)
locked <- names(renv::lockfile_read('renv.lock')$Packages)
base_pkgs <- rownames(installed.packages(priority = 'base'))
missing <- setdiff(used, c(locked, base_pkgs))
if (length(missing) > 0) {
  stop('Used in analysis/ but not pinned in renv.lock: ',
       toString(missing))
}
```

A companion tool, `zzrenvcheck`, does the same scan with
more care (tests, vignettes, version constraints, and the
stricter `DESCRIPTION` inclusion for the package
archetype), and in CI it must be called with
`error_on_fail = TRUE`, so that a failed check stops the
step with a nonzero exit status rather than printing a
report and exiting cleanly. It is not on CRAN, so the
workflow installs it explicitly. Either form catches the
most common and most insidious drift of all: a package
installed interactively during analysis, used in the code,
and never snapshotted, so that the lockfile is silently
incomplete.

A condensed GitHub Actions workflow that runs the three
gates on every push and pull request illustrates the
shape of the thing. It uses the R community's
`r-lib/actions` for the setup and the check, at the major
versions current when this chapter was revised
(`actions/checkout@v7`, `r-lib/actions/*@v2`). We show it
as a static file: its YAML was checked for syntax, and the
command in each gate was run against a toy compendium, but
the workflow as a whole is executed by the CI service,
never by this book.

```yaml
name: compendium

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  gates:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    env:
      GITHUB_PAT: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # Install the R version recorded in renv.lock.
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-r@v2
        with:
          r-version: renv
          use-public-rspm: true

      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-pandoc@v2

      # Restore renv.lock into the project library. The
      # project's .Rprofile activates that library in
      # every later R step run from the repository root.
      - uses: r-lib/actions/setup-renv@v2

      # The gate tools are not analysis dependencies, so
      # they are installed here rather than pinned.
      - name: Install the gate tools
        shell: Rscript {0}
        run: |
          renv::install(c('rcmdcheck', 'remotes', 'pkgload'))
          remotes::install_github('rgt47/zzrenvcheck')

      # Gate 1: R CMD check of the package skin. Any
      # WARNING, such as an undeclared import, fails.
      - uses: r-lib/actions/check-r-package@v2
        with:
          args: 'c("--no-manual")'
          error-on: '"warning"'

      # Gate 2: every package the code uses, analysis/
      # included, is declared and pinned.
      - name: Dependency-manifest gate
        shell: Rscript {0}
        run: |
          zzrenvcheck::check_packages(strict = TRUE,
                                      error_on_fail = TRUE)

      # Gate 3: the report re-renders from source.
      - name: Render gate
        shell: Rscript {0}
        run: |
          rmarkdown::render('analysis/report/report.Rmd',
                            output_format = 'html_document',
                            output_dir = tempdir())
```

Three choices in the file deserve a word. `error-on` is
set to `"warning"` explicitly, although that is also the
action's default, because the setting is the whole
difference between a gate that catches an undeclared
import and one that does not. The render gate renders to
HTML into a temporary folder: it tests that every chunk
runs, and leaves PDF typesetting, which needs a LaTeX
installation, to a separate step if the deliverable is a
PDF. And nothing in the file is marked
`continue-on-error`; a step that is allowed to fail
without failing the job is a report, not a gate.

The house rule of this book is that a gate is not shown to
work until it has been seen to fail. Each of the three can
be turned red on purpose, in a branch, in a few minutes:

| Gate | Deliberate breakage | What the run reports |
|---|---|---|
| `R CMD check` | Call `sandwich::vcovHC()` in a function in `R/` without adding `sandwich` to `DESCRIPTION` | A WARNING, '`::` or `:::` import not declared from', which `error-on: '"warning"'` turns into a failed step |
| Dependency manifest | Add `library(sandwich)` to a script in `analysis/` without snapshotting | The missing package is listed and the step stops with an error |
| Render | Add a chunk that loads a package absent from `renv.lock`, or uses an object no chunk creates | `rmarkdown::render()` stops at that chunk and names it |

We ran each breakage against a toy compendium (R 4.6.1,
`rcmdcheck` 1.4.0, `zzrenvcheck` from its source
repository in October 2026), and each command exited with a
nonzero status. The first breakage also shows why the
setting matters: with `error_on = "error"` the same check
returned normally, the WARNING printed and ignored.
Placing `library(sandwich)` in `analysis/` rather than in
`R/` shows the scope of the first gate: `R CMD check`
passes, the dependency gate goes red, and the render gate
goes red too if the report runs that script.

### Where CI bugs hide: cross-boundary state

The reader will have noticed, in the workflow above, an
apparently pedantic care over where the pinned library is
restored and from which directory each R step starts. This
is not pedantry; it avoids a subtle and instructive bug,
and the lesson generalizes well beyond the particular case.

The trouble is that a CI run is not one continuous
process but a sequence of separate steps, each a fresh
shell, and within a step the check itself runs in a
further separate subprocess. State does not automatically
cross these boundaries. In one documented case, the step
that restored the pinned packages installed them
correctly, and the very next step, running `R CMD check`,
reported a required package as 'not available'. The
package was on disk; the check simply could not see where.
Two boundaries conspired. The restore step adjusted the
library path in its own shell, but the next step is a
fresh shell and inherited none of that. And even within
a step, `R CMD check` runs in a child subprocess whose
library path must be passed to it explicitly, because
adjusting the path in the calling session does not
propagate to the child. The fix is to launch the check
from a session in which the restored library is already
on the library path, and to make sure that path travels
to the child. In the workflow above, `setup-renv` restores
into the project library; every later R step starts in the
repository root, where the project's `.Rprofile` activates
that library; and `rcmdcheck()` hands the calling
session's `.libPaths()` to the check subprocess, which is
the default of its `libpath` argument. A workflow that
restores into some other folder must pass that folder to
`libpath` by hand.

What makes the episode instructive is why it stayed
hidden. The workflow had passed for several repositories,
because each of them imported only packages that the
generic container base image already provided; the
restored library was never actually needed. The defect
surfaced only when a repository imported a specialized
modeling package absent from the base image. The broader
literature on why deposited analyses fail to re-run
[@trisovic2022] documents how often re-execution simply
fails. The particular fault here is cross-boundary state,
the state that must pass from one step, shell, or process
to the next and silently does not. It is where CI bugs
hide, and a
dormant defect of this kind needs an adversarial input,
a dependency outside the comfortable base image, to bring
it to light. The general moral is one this book returns
to: a check that passes tells you only that it was not
exercised hard enough to fail.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: capture versus validation

A colleague proposes to save CI minutes by deleting the
continuous-integration workflow from a compendium that
already has a committed `renv.lock` and `Dockerfile`.
They argue that since the lockfile and the container
'contain the reproducibility', removing CI cannot lower
the compendium's reproducibility level. Are they correct
about the level? Are they correct that nothing is lost?

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

They are correct about the level and wrong about the
loss. The reproducibility level is set by what is
captured: the lockfile pins the packages (L1) and the
container pins the environment (L2). Continuous
integration captures nothing, so removing it leaves the
compendium at exactly the level it held before, L2. What
is lost is not level but assurance. Without CI, no one
tests, on a clean machine, that the captured environment
still rebuilds. The compendium becomes trusted rather
than tested, and the silent decay of an external
reference, a package pulled from its repository, a base
image whose digest drifts, will go unnoticed until
someone tries a rebuild by hand. The colleague has
correctly identified that CI is validation, not capture,
and drawn precisely the wrong conclusion from it.
:::
:::

## Two dialects: GitHub Actions and GitLab CI

Continuous integration is a general idea with several
implementations, and a health researcher should know at
least two, because the choice is often not theirs to make.
GitHub Actions and GitLab CI are two dialects of the same
underlying activity, and the difference between them is
one of syntax and hosting, not of principle.

The forge, the platform hosting the repository, matters
for research in a way it does not for general software
development. Research compendia are disproportionately
authored on institutional, often self-hosted, GitLab.
Many universities and laboratories, particularly in
Europe and wherever data-governance rules discourage
commercial cloud hosting, run their own GitLab servers
and cannot, or will not, push a repository to github.com.
For a clinical or registry study whose data-handling
agreement forbids external hosting, the ability to run the
same reproducibility checks on institutional GitLab is not
a convenience but a precondition. A framework that assumed
GitHub would simply be unavailable to a large part of its
intended audience.

The two dialects differ structurally. GitHub Actions uses
one or more workflow files under `.github/workflows/`, each
organized into jobs and, within a job, a sequence of named
steps. GitLab CI uses a single `.gitlab-ci.yml` organized
into stages, each stage running a script. The same three
gates, expressed in the GitLab dialect, look like this,
again shown as a static file that GitLab executes and this
book does not:

```yaml
stages:
  - gates
  - verify

gates:
  stage: gates
  # The tag must name the R version recorded in renv.lock.
  image: rocker/verse:4.4.0
  script:
    - Rscript -e 'renv::restore(prompt = FALSE)'
    - Rscript -e 'renv::install(c("rcmdcheck", "remotes",
        "pkgload"))'
    - Rscript -e 'remotes::install_github("rgt47/zzrenvcheck")'
    # Gate 1: R CMD check of the package skin
    - Rscript -e 'rcmdcheck::rcmdcheck(args = "--no-manual",
        error_on = "warning")'
    # Gate 2: the dependency manifest, analysis/ included
    - Rscript -e 'zzrenvcheck::check_packages(strict = TRUE,
        error_on_fail = TRUE)'
    # Gate 3: the report re-renders from source
    - Rscript -e 'rmarkdown::render(
        "analysis/report/report.Rmd",
        output_format = "html_document",
        output_dir = tempdir())'

verify:
  stage: verify
  # A shell-executor runner with Docker installed; the
  # tag is whatever the institution assigns to it.
  tags: [docker-shell]
  script:
    - docker build -t compendium:ci .
    - docker run --rm -e RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED=FALSE
        -v "$PWD":/work -w /work
        compendium:ci Rscript ci/run-tests.R
```

The two files say the same thing in different words: run
on the R version the lockfile records, restore the pinned
library into the project library, install the gate tools
beside it, and run the three gates from the repository
root, so that every R step, and the check subprocess it
launches, sees the restored library. The `rocker/verse`
image is used on GitLab because it ships pandoc, which the
render gate needs; on GitHub the `setup-pandoc` action
supplies it. Each script line is a separate shell command,
and GitLab fails the job at the first one that exits with a
nonzero status, so every gate here can fail the pipeline.
The second job, `verify`, which rebuilds the project image
and runs the baseline tests inside it, is the subject of
the next section; on GitLab it needs a runner that can
build images, which is an institutional decision, since
the common alternative, Docker-in-Docker, requires a
privileged runner that many institutions do not allow.
On the plus side, maintaining a repository on
whichever forge an institution mandates is then a matter of
translating the dialect rather than abandoning the checks.
On the minus side, a workflow written twice, once per
dialect, is a workflow maintained twice, and every future
change must be made in two incompatible formats, a
standing divergence hazard. The resolution a mature
framework adopts is to single-source the logic in a
neutral place, the project's own `Makefile`, with one
target per gate (say `check`, `deps`, and `render`)
holding the commands shown above, so that each forge's CI file
shrinks to a thin shim that checks out the code and calls
`make`. The dialect then differs only in its outermost ten
lines, and the checking behavior is defined once.

A further design point is that a workflow can adapt
itself to what the repository contains rather than being
configured by hand. A feature is treated as present
exactly when its defining file exists. If `renv.lock` is
present, the workflow restores the pinned library;
otherwise it installs from `DESCRIPTION`. If a `Dockerfile`
or a Nix `flake.nix` is present, the workflow builds and
runs inside that environment; otherwise it runs on the
host runner. Such a workflow survives a project's toggling
of `renv` or of its container backend with no edit, and
one file can serve every archetype and every capture
level. The workflows in this chapter are not written that
way: they assume a compendium with both a lockfile and a
`Dockerfile`, so that every step is visible. A
presence-driven workflow wraps each step in a condition,
in GitHub's dialect `if: hashFiles('Dockerfile') != ''`,
and that convenience has a cost the reader should weigh: a
condition is also a way for a gate to disappear without
notice, since a misnamed file switches the step off and
the run stays green. A workflow that adapts should
therefore print which gates it ran and which it skipped.

## Verification and level L3

We have reached the top of the ladder. The first three
gates confirm that the compendium builds, checks, and
renders on a clean machine. They do not confirm that it
produces the *same numbers*. That is the work of
verification, the L2-to-L3 transition, and it proceeds
not by capturing more but by confirming what has been
captured.

L3, as @sec-levels defines it, requires that recorded
outputs be shown to regenerate within a stated tolerance
from a clean rebuild. Each part of that sentence names a
mechanism. The recorded outputs and the tolerance live in
a *baseline test* (@sec-testing): a committed file of key
estimates, recorded once, and a test file named
`test-baseline-*.R` that recomputes them and compares with
`expect_equal(..., tolerance = ...)`. The clean rebuild is
the project's own image, built from its `Dockerfile` on a
machine that has never seen it. Verification is running
the first inside the second, and it fails if either
fails: if the image does not rebuild, if any test fails,
or if no baseline test runs at all. A test suite without
a baseline test can pass in a rebuilt image and show that
the environment is sound, which is L2 confirmed, but it
has compared nothing with a recorded result, so it is not
L3.

In continuous integration this is a second job in the same
workflow, run after the gates pass:

```yaml
  verify:
    needs: gates
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7

      # L2: the project's own Dockerfile must rebuild.
      - name: Rebuild the project image
        run: docker build -t compendium:ci .

      # L3: the test suite, with at least one baseline
      # test, must pass inside the rebuilt image.
      - name: Run the tests in the image
        run: >
          docker run --rm
          -e RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED=FALSE
          -v "$PWD":/work -w /work
          compendium:ci Rscript ci/run-tests.R
```

The test step runs a short script from the repository,
because the obvious one-line call,
`tinytest::run_test_dir('inst/tinytest')`, returns its
results and exits with status 0 even when an expectation
fails; we confirmed this with a deliberately failing test.
The script turns failures into a nonzero exit, and also
refuses to pass if no baseline test produced a result,
which is the case when the baseline file is missing or
when its guard found no data and exited early:

```r
# ci/run-tests.R
pkgload::load_all('.', quiet = TRUE)
res <- tinytest::run_test_dir('inst/tinytest')
print(res)
ran <- unique(as.data.frame(res)$file)
if (!any(grepl('^test-baseline', ran))) {
  stop('No baseline test ran, so this is not an L3 check.')
}
if (!tinytest::all_pass(res)) quit(status = 1)
```

Two assumptions are built in and should be checked against
the reader's own image. The image must contain `tinytest`
and `pkgload`, which means they must be in the lockfile it
restores. And it must put the pinned library on R's path
without the project's `.Rprofile`, for instance in the site
library, because the environment variable
`RENV_CONFIG_AUTOLOADER_ENABLED=FALSE` stops the mounted
project from activating a project library that does not
exist inside the container. The house rule applies here as
well. Changing one value in the committed baseline file
by more than the tolerance turns the job red at the
baseline expectation; deleting or renaming the
`test-baseline-*.R` file turns it red at the 'no baseline
test ran' check; and breaking a `RUN` line in the
`Dockerfile` turns it red at the build. Against the toy
compendium, outside a container, we ran the first two, and
also a baseline file whose guard found no data and exited
early; each run of the script exited with status 1, and
the unbroken run exited with 0. The image build and the
job as a whole were not run for this chapter.

In the framework this book uses, the same composition is
the command `zzc verify`, which runs in two tiers. A
default *coherence* tier requires no rebuild: it checks
that the captured artifacts agree with each other, that the
R version named in the lockfile matches the one in the
Dockerfile, that the backend is unambiguous, and that the
raw data still matches its recorded checksums. A `--full`
*reproduction* tier rebuilds the image, runs the test
suite inside it, and stamps L3 into the project's state
record only when three things hold: the image rebuilt, the
tests passed, and at least one `inst/tinytest/test-baseline*.R`
file exists and ran. Without a baseline test it reports
the project as rebuilt and tested, at L2, with no baseline
comparison, and does not stamp L3. Any later change to the
environment drops the stamp, so a compendium that has
drifted reverts to unverified automatically, rather than
carrying a stale claim.

Here is the subtle and important point, and it is worth
dwelling on. Verification compares **computational
outputs**, the row count of a derived dataset, a fitted
coefficient, a bootstrap bound, and *not* the rendered PDF
or HTML. The reason is that a rendered document is not a
deterministic function of the analysis. As @sec-literate
discussed, a PDF embeds the time of its creation and the
identifiers of the fonts the rendering machine happened to
have. Two renders of an unchanged analysis, minutes apart,
produce PDFs whose bytes differ, even though every number
in them is identical. Comparing PDFs would therefore
report a difference on every render and catch nothing real.
Comparing the estimates themselves, within a tolerance,
reports a difference exactly when a number changed by more
than floating-point noise, which is what we want to
detect. A hash is the right instrument for a file whose
bytes should not change, such as a raw data extract (the
next section); it is the wrong one for an estimate, whose
last binary digit can move under a different BLAS without
the analysis changing. There exist techniques to normalize
a document's embedded timestamps, by setting a fixed
`SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH`, and to freeze its fonts, and with
enough care a byte-identical PDF is attainable. But the
robust and general practice is to verify the computational
outputs directly and leave the document to the render
gate.

::: {.callout-important}
## The honest level

Verification is the one rung of the ladder that cannot be
claimed on trust. An analyst may reasonably state that a
compendium is at L1 by pointing to a lockfile, or at L2 by
pointing to a pinned image, because those artifacts exist
and can be inspected. But a claim of L3 asserts that the
outputs have been regenerated in a clean rebuild and shown
to match a committed baseline within a stated tolerance,
and that claim is only as good as an actual, recent,
successful verification run that included a baseline test. A `verified` stamp that predates the
last change to the environment is not an L3 claim; it is a
stale one. Match the claim to the level actually reached,
and let the stamp expire when the environment moves beneath
it.
:::

## Data integrity: the checksum manifest

One input sits outside everything the lockfile and the
container pin: the raw data itself. A container fixes the
software that reads the data, and a lockfile fixes the
packages, but neither notices if the data file on disk is
silently altered, a row edited, a value corrected, a
column recoded, between the analysis and its re-execution.
An altered input produces a changed result with no error
and no warning, the quietest reproducibility failure of
all.

The guard is a **checksum manifest**, a small file,
conventionally `data-manifest.sha256`, that records the
SHA-256 checksum of each raw data file. Verification reads
the manifest, recomputes the checksum of each file as it
now stands, and reports a mismatch. Because any change to
a file's bytes changes its checksum, a silently altered
input is caught the next time verification runs.

The mechanism is easiest to see on a small synthetic
example. We construct a tiny derived dataset, record its
checksum, alter a single value, and recompute. The point
to observe is that a one-cell change, a shift of a single
outcome from 11.1 to 11.2, produces a completely different
digest, so the alteration cannot pass unnoticed.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-integrity
#| tbl-cap: 'A single altered value changes the digest of a derived dataset. The two frames differ in exactly one cell, yet their SHA-256 digests differ from the first character, so a checksum manifest detects the change.'
library(tibble)
library(digest)
library(knitr)

cohort <- tibble(
  id      = 1:5,
  arm     = c('treatment', 'placebo', 'treatment',
              'placebo', 'treatment'),
  outcome = c(12.4, 9.8, 11.1, 10.3, 13.0)
)

baseline <- digest(cohort, algo = 'sha256')

altered <- cohort
altered$outcome[3] <- 11.2
altered_digest <- digest(altered, algo = 'sha256')

manifest <- tibble(
  object = c('cohort (baseline)',
             'cohort (one cell altered)'),
  digest_first16 = c(substr(baseline, 1, 16),
                     substr(altered_digest, 1, 16)),
  matches_baseline = c('yes', 'no')
)

kable(
  manifest,
  col.names = c('Object', 'SHA-256 (first 16 chars)',
                'Matches baseline'),
  align = 'llc'
)
```

The two digests differ from the first character despite
the frames differing in a single cell. This is the property
that makes a checksum a reliable integrity guard: it is
sensitive to any change and indifferent to none. A
verification run that recomputes these digests and finds
the second where it expected the first has caught an
altered input, and has done so without needing to know
what the correct value was, only that it has changed since
the manifest was recorded.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Check your understanding: what to hash

A student proposes to verify their manuscript compendium
by recording the SHA-256 checksum of the rendered
`report.pdf` and re-checking it on every rebuild. They
reason that if the PDF is byte-identical, the whole
analysis must have reproduced. Identify the flaw, and say
what they should hash instead.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Answer

The flaw is that a rendered PDF is not a deterministic
function of the analysis. It embeds the time of rendering
and the identifiers of the fonts on the rendering machine,
so two renders of an unchanged analysis produce PDFs with
different bytes and therefore different checksums. The
student's check would report a failure on every single
rebuild, catching nothing real and quickly training them
to ignore it. They should instead check the computational
outputs that feed the report: the estimates and the key
counts, compared with a committed baseline within a stated
tolerance by a baseline test, and, where a derived file's
bytes should not change, its checksum. The render gate,
separately, confirms that the document still builds from
those outputs. Byte-identical PDFs are attainable with
timestamp normalization and font freezing, but that is a
fragile route to a result the baseline test gives
directly.
:::
:::

## Proving the framework itself: the capture test matrix

There is a question one rung below the compendium's own
verification, and it is easy to overlook: how does the
framework know that a project configured for, say, L1
actually reaches L1? A claim that a given combination of
toggles produces a given level is itself a claim that can
be tested, and a responsible framework tests it rather
than asserting it.

The instrument is a **capture test matrix**. It scaffolds
a throwaway compendium for each combination of the capture
axes, the package backend present or absent, the container
environment present or absent, and asserts, for each, that
the result passes `R CMD check`, is a loadable workspace,
and sits at its stated level. The matrix has the following
shape, with the axes being the capture axes and CI serving
as the harness that runs the matrix rather than a dimension
of it.

| Backend (`renv`) | Environment (Docker) | Level | Assertion |
|---|---|---|---|
| off | off | L0 | check passes; valid workspace |
| on  | off | L1 | check passes; `renv` activates on host |
| off | on  | L2 | check passes; image installs from `DESCRIPTION` |
| on  | on  | L2 | check passes; image restores from lockfile |

Two points about the matrix deserve emphasis. First, Nix,
the alternative backend of @sec-backends, is verified as a
*substitution*: because it replaces the `renv`-plus-Docker
combination and must reach L2 on its own, it is checked as
a peer of that combination rather than added as a fourth
column. Second, the configuration that renders a report
with `renv` on but Docker off is, in practice, the most
error-prone, and it is exercised explicitly rather than
left to chance. Because container builds under emulation
are expensive, the matrix is tiered: the host-only rows run
on every pull request, and the rows that build an image run
on merge and on a nightly schedule. This is the framework
turning its own machinery on itself, and it is the same
move, at one level of remove, as a compendium verifying its
own outputs.

## How continuous integration adapts to the archetype

We have stressed throughout the book that a research
compendium is not only a manuscript. It comes in several
archetypes, and continuous integration adapts to each,
because the gates that make sense depend on what the
compendium is for. Of the three gates of this chapter, two
are universal and one is archetype-conditional. `R CMD
check` is universal, inherited by every archetype by virtue
of the R-package skin they all share. The
dependency-manifest gate is likewise run everywhere, though
in its archetype-conditional form: the strict
`DESCRIPTION`-inclusion check applies to the R-package
archetype, while a compendium enforces only the weaker
$\mathrm{Code} \subseteq \mathrm{renv.lock}$ inclusion, as
the first section established. The render gate is the
conditional one, added wherever the compendium carries a
report and omitted where it does not. Verification, the L3
step of the previous section, is not one of the three
build-time gates but a further act layered on top wherever
a recorded numeric baseline exists.

An **R-package archetype**, a reusable set of functions
destined perhaps for CRAN, has no report to render. Its CI
runs `R CMD check` and the unit-test suite (@sec-testing),
and that is the whole of it; imposing a render gate on it
would be imposing a gate on a document that does not exist.

A **manuscript archetype** and a **blog archetype** both
add the render gate, because both center on a rendered
document, a `report.Rmd` for the manuscript, a set of
posts for the blog. The blog case merely renders many
documents rather than one; the render gate iterates over
every post under the posts directory. For these archetypes
the render gate is not optional decoration but the check
that the reader-facing artifact still regenerates from its
source.

A **data-analysis archetype** sits between them: it may
carry a report or may organize its work as scripts and
figures with no single manuscript, and its CI is
configured accordingly. A **simulation archetype** raises
a distinct concern of cost. A simulation study whose full
run takes hours or days cannot run in its entirety on every
push. The idiomatic arrangement is to run a *reduced*
pipeline under CI, a handful of iterations with a fixed
seed, enough to confirm that the pipeline executes and the
outputs have the right shape, and to run the full pipeline
elsewhere, on a cluster or a scheduled long-running job,
with its results verified against a baseline separately.
The seeding discipline of @sec-testing is what makes the
reduced run meaningful: a fixed seed makes even a short run
reproducible, so that CI checks reproducibility rather than
merely execution.

The general principle is that the archetype selects the
gates, and the presence-driven workflow discovers the
archetype from what the repository contains. A report file
present means the render gate applies; absent, it does not.
The analyst's contribution, as stated at the outset, is to
ensure the archetype and its gates are matched, so that CI
tests what the compendium actually is.

## Independent external verification

The checking we have described so far is the author's own,
run on the author's forge against the author's baseline. It
is necessary and it is not sufficient, because an author
who has misunderstood their own reproducibility can build a
CI pipeline that faithfully confirms the misunderstanding.
The complement is verification from outside the project
entirely, by someone with no stake in its passing.

The most developed such scheme is CODECHECK, described by
Nust and Eglen [@nust2021codecheck], in which an
independent codechecker re-executes an analysis during peer
review, on their own machine, and issues a certificate
recording what was run and what was reproduced. The value
of the exercise lies exactly in its independence: the
codechecker carries none of the author's undeclared state,
which is the same property that makes a CI runner effective,
now embodied in a person rather than a virtual machine. In
a parallel development, major computing venues have
formalized artifact review and badging, under which a
submission's computational artifacts are evaluated and, if
they reproduce, marked with a badge on the published paper
[@acm2020]. Stodden and colleagues have documented both the
persistence of the reproducibility problem and the
effectiveness, and limits, of journal policies that attempt
to compel deposition and checking [@stodden2018], and the
ten-rules literature places independent re-execution among
its recommendations [@sandve2013].

These schemes validate; they do not capture. They add no
lockfile and no container. What they add is a second, and
independent, execution of the analysis, and in doing so
they extend the logic of this chapter to its natural
conclusion. Continuous integration is a machine that is not
yours; independent verification is a person who is not you;
and both catch, at the last responsible moment before a
result enters the scientific record, the reproducibility
failures that the author's own generous machine had hidden.

## Worked example

To make the machinery concrete, consider a plausible
sequence of events in a cohort-study compendium, of the
kind that recurs in practice.

The analyst is refining a model and, mid-session, reaches
for a package that computes robust standard errors,
`sandwich`. They install it interactively with
`install.packages()`, add `library(sandwich)` to
`analysis/scripts/02_model.R`, which the report sources,
obtain the result they wanted, and commit. On their own
machine everything runs: the package is installed, the
script loads it, the report renders, the numbers appear.
The compendium looks, to its author, finished.

The push triggers CI, and the fresh runner tells a
different story, though not at the gate a reader might
expect. The runner checks out the committed files and
restores the pinned library from `renv.lock`, the lockfile
that was never updated because the interactive install
was never snapshotted. Gate 1, `R CMD check`, passes. It
is not at fault: the script lives in `analysis/`, which
the build excludes, so the check never reads it. Gate 2,
the dependency-manifest gate, reads `analysis/` and goes
red, naming `sandwich` as a package the code uses and the
lockfile does not pin. Had that gate been absent, gate 3
would have failed the same run from the other direction:
the report sources the script, the script calls
`library(sandwich)`, and the restored library has no such
package, so the render stops at that chunk. Either way, CI
has found on a clean machine precisely the undeclared
state the author's machine supplied silently. Had the
workflow run only `R CMD check`, as many compendium
workflows do, the build would have been green.

The fix is not to weaken the check but to repair the
capture. The analyst records the new package in the
lockfile by snapshotting the environment, commits the
updated `renv.lock`, and pushes again. This time the
runner restores a library that contains the package, the
dependency gate passes, the report renders, and the gates
go green. The `verify` job then rebuilds the image from
the new lockfile and runs the baseline test, which is
where the analyst learns whether the change moved a
recorded result, such as a confidence limit; if it did,
the baseline is
re-recorded deliberately, in a commit that says why, not
loosened until it passes. The episode is the whole
argument of the chapter in miniature: the failure was
real, it was caused by undeclared state, it was invisible
on the author's machine, it was caught only by a gate that
looks where the defect was, and it was caught by a machine
that was not the author's, at the last moment before the
incomplete compendium could reach anyone else.

## Collaborating with an LLM

A large language model is a capable assistant for CI work,
which is heavy on boilerplate YAML, and a hazardous one,
because CI failures are subtle and a plausible-looking
workflow can be quietly wrong. We give three prompt
patterns, each with what to watch for and what the analyst
must independently verify.

CI touches data in ways that are easy to miss, so one rule
comes first. Never paste or upload protected health
information, identifiable records, or data covered by a
data-use agreement, nor outputs derived from them, into a
model unless your institution has approved that endpoint
for that data; a CI log that prints rows of a failing
render or test is such an output. Describe the structure
instead: the workflow file, the error message, column
names and types, a synthetic example. A coding agent
reads the files in its repository, so run one only in a
compendium whose data it is permitted to see.

**Prompt.** 'Write a GitHub Actions workflow that runs `R
CMD check` on my compendium inside the `rocker/tidyverse`
container and restores packages from `renv.lock`.'

*Watch for.* A workflow that restores the library in one
step and runs the check in another without ensuring the
restored library reaches the check subprocess. As we saw,
adjusting the library path in one step does not carry to
the next, and `R CMD check` runs in a child process that
sees only the library path it is handed. A model will
frequently produce the naive two-step form that passes
only when every dependency happens to be in the base
image. Watch also for `error_on = "error"`, a dependency
step that reports without failing, and
`continue-on-error: true`, each of which leaves a gate
that cannot go red; and remember that `R CMD check` alone
never looks at `analysis/`.

*Verification.* Do not trust the workflow because it is
syntactically valid. Confirm it fails correctly by
introducing a deliberate gap, importing a specialized
package absent from the base image and not restoring it,
and checking that the build goes red. A CI check that has
never been seen to fail has not been shown to work.

**Prompt.** 'Add a verification step that checks my analysis
reproduces, by hashing the output and comparing it to a
saved value.'

*Watch for.* A step that hashes the rendered PDF or HTML.
The model will often reach for the most visible output, the
report, which is exactly the wrong thing to hash because its
bytes carry timestamps and font identifiers and change on
every render.

*Verification.* Insist that the target is a computational
output, and that estimates are compared with a committed
baseline within a stated tolerance, in a
`test-baseline-*.R` file, while hashes are kept for files
whose bytes should not change. Confirm by rendering the
report twice without changing the analysis: the report's
own bytes should differ while the baseline test still
passes. If the model's chosen target changes between the
two renders, it is the wrong target.

**Prompt.** 'My compendium is a simulation study that takes
six hours to run. Write CI for it.'

*Watch for.* A workflow that attempts the full run on every
push, which will time out or consume the CI budget, or one
that runs so few iterations that it no longer tests
anything meaningful.

*Verification.* Confirm the workflow runs a reduced,
fixed-seed pipeline under CI and defers the full run
elsewhere, and check that the reduced run is seeded so that
its short output is itself reproducible. Verify that the
number of iterations in the reduced run is large enough to
exercise the code paths that matter, not merely one.

In every case the pattern is the same. The model is
competent at the syntax and unreliable about the semantics,
and the semantics, what the check actually proves and
whether it can fail for the right reason, are exactly what
the analyst must verify and cannot delegate.

## Exercises

1. **Capture versus validation.** In your own words,
   explain why removing a continuous-integration workflow
   from a compendium does not lower its position on the
   reproducibility ladder, and state precisely what is lost
   when CI is removed. Give one concrete failure that CI
   would have caught and that its absence now permits to go
   unnoticed.

2. **The three gates.** For each of the three CI gates
   (`R CMD check`, the render gate, the dependency-manifest
   gate), describe a specific defect in a compendium that
   the gate catches and the other two do not. Then name one
   reproducibility failure that none of the three catches,
   and say which gate, verification or data integrity,
   addresses it.

3. **What to hash.** Take the code in @tbl-integrity as a
   starting point. Extend it to hash a small linear model
   object fitted to the synthetic `cohort` data with
   `lm(outcome ~ arm, data = cohort)`, record the digest,
   refit the identical model, and confirm the digest is
   unchanged. Then alter one outcome value, refit, and
   confirm the digest changes. Explain why hashing the model
   object is a sound verification target whereas hashing a
   plot of the model would not be.

4. **Two dialects.** Take the condensed GitHub Actions
   workflow shown in this chapter and translate it into the
   equivalent `.gitlab-ci.yml`. Identify the two structural
   differences between the dialects (jobs-and-steps versus
   stages-and-scripts, and per-file versus single-file
   configuration), and explain why single-sourcing the
   check logic in a `Makefile` would let both files shrink
   to a thin shim.

5. **Archetype and gates.** For each of the five archetypes
   (data analysis, manuscript, R package, simulation, blog),
   state which of the three CI gates apply and why. For the
   simulation archetype, describe specifically how you would
   arrange a reduced pipeline under CI and a full pipeline
   elsewhere, and what role a fixed seed plays in making the
   reduced run a genuine reproducibility test.

6. **Independent verification.** Read the CODECHECK
   description of Nust and Eglen [@nust2021codecheck].
   Explain in what respect an independent codechecker plays
   the same role, for a submitted analysis, that a CI runner
   plays for a committed change. Then identify one class of
   reproducibility failure that an independent human
   codechecker would catch and that the author's own CI,
   however well configured, cannot.

## Solutions

Attempt an exercise before expanding its solution. Exercises
3 and 4 are hands-on and their outputs will vary; the boxes
record the expected result and the reasoning.

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 1

The ladder grades **capture**: how far down the determinant
stack a result is locked. CI locks nothing. It installs no
package into the lockfile and no library into the image, so
removing it leaves every pinned layer exactly as pinned as
before. A compendium at L2 with CI and the same compendium
at L2 without it sit on the same rung.

**What is lost is assurance rather than level.** Without CI
nobody rebuilds the captured environment on a clean machine
and re-runs the analysis in it. The compendium becomes
trusted rather than tested, and the distance between 'this
should rebuild' and 'this does rebuild' stops being
measured.

**A concrete failure.** A base image is repointed by its
maintainer and the Dockerfile pins it by tag rather than
digest, so the environment quietly changes underneath the
project. With CI, the next push rebuilds and the check
fails, naming the day it broke. Without CI, the compendium
looks healthy on the author's machine, where an old image
is cached locally, and fails for the first reader who
builds it from scratch, possibly years later, with no
indication of when or why it broke. Equally good answers:
a package pulled from CRAN and no longer restorable, a
system library the analysis silently depended on and never
declared, or a chunk that only ever ran because of state
left in the author's session.

The general shape of the loss is that decay is silent and
CI is what makes it loud.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 2

**`R CMD check`** catches a defect in the package skin as
code: a function in `R/` calling a package that is used but
not declared in `DESCRIPTION` (a WARNING, so the gate must
fail on warnings), a syntax error in a file under `R/` that
nothing currently calls, a documented argument that no
longer exists. The render gate would not see it if the
report does not touch that function, and the manifest gate
checks declarations rather than whether the code loads.
The same defects under `analysis/` are invisible to
`R CMD check`, which never sees that directory.

**The render gate** catches a defect that appears only when
the document is built: a chunk that fails on a clean
machine because it read an uncommitted file, a figure whose
code errors, a cross-reference to a label that no longer
exists. `R CMD check` never renders, so it sees none of
this.

**The dependency-manifest gate** catches drift between the
three manifests: a package used in the code and absent
from `DESCRIPTION`, or declared in `DESCRIPTION` and
missing from `renv.lock`. The code may load and the
document may render perfectly on a machine where the
package happens to be installed, so neither other gate
fires.

**A failure none of the three catches:** a change in the
*data*. A raw extract silently replaced with a corrected
version leaves the code valid, the document renderable,
and the manifests consistent, while every number in the
report changes. All three gates pass. The **data-integrity
gate** addresses it, by hashing the inputs and derived
outputs and comparing against a recorded manifest.

The **verification gate** addresses the adjacent case in
which the code changes a result without any of the three
noticing, by comparing computed outputs against recorded
baselines.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 3

```r
library(digest)
m1 <- lm(outcome ~ arm, data = cohort)
d1 <- digest(coef(m1), algo = 'sha256')

m2 <- lm(outcome ~ arm, data = cohort)
digest(coef(m2), algo = 'sha256') == d1     # TRUE

cohort$outcome[1] <- cohort$outcome[1] + 1
m3 <- lm(outcome ~ arm, data = cohort)
digest(coef(m3), algo = 'sha256') == d1     # FALSE
```

Refitting the identical model to identical data gives an
identical digest; altering one outcome value changes it.

**Why the model object is a sound target.** The
coefficients are a deterministic function of the data and
the model specification. Nothing about the time of
fitting, the machine's fonts, or the session's history
enters them. So the digest changes exactly when a number
changes and not otherwise, which is what makes a failure
informative.

One practical refinement the exercise invites. Digesting
the whole `lm` object rather than `coef()` is fragile,
because the object stores the call and a `terms`
environment, which can carry incidental references. Hashing
the coefficient vector, or a named list of the quantities
actually reported, is the more robust choice.

**Why hashing a plot would not be sound.** A rendered plot
is an image file, and image files embed creation
timestamps, are affected by device version and font
availability, and can differ in their compression between
runs. Two plots of the identical model can differ byte for
byte while depicting exactly the same thing, so the check
would fail on every rebuild and carry no information. The
rule this generalizes to is that verification hashes
computational outputs, not rendered artifacts, and it is
the same rule that governs the PDF in @sec-literate.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 4

```yaml
# .gitlab-ci.yml
stages: [check]

check:
  stage: check
  image: rocker/verse:4.4.0
  script:
    - make check
    - make render
    - make check-renv
```

**The two structural differences.**

*Jobs and steps versus stages and scripts.* GitHub Actions
composes a job from reusable `uses:` steps, each a
versioned action maintained elsewhere, so the workflow
reads as an assembly of components. GitLab CI defines
stages containing jobs whose bodies are shell scripts, so
the pipeline reads as commands in an image. The GitHub
form is more declarative and depends on an ecosystem of
actions; the GitLab form is more direct and depends on
nothing but the image.

*Per-file versus single-file configuration.* GitHub reads
every file under `.github/workflows/`, so a project
naturally accumulates several workflows with separate
triggers. GitLab reads a single `.gitlab-ci.yml` at the
root, so everything is expressed in one file with rules
selecting what runs when.

**Why a Makefile shrinks both.** The differences above are
entirely about *orchestration*: what runs, in what order,
on what trigger. The check logic itself, run `R CMD check`,
render the report, verify the manifests, is identical in
both and belongs in neither file. Putting it behind
`make check`, `make render`, and `make check-renv` leaves
each CI file a thin shim naming the image and calling
three targets. The logic is then single-sourced, testable
locally with the same command CI runs, and portable to a
third forge for the cost of one more shim.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 5

**Data analysis:** `R CMD check` and the manifest gate
always; the render gate if a report is produced.
**Manuscript:** all three, since the rendered document is
the deliverable. **R package:** `R CMD check` and the
manifest gate; the render gate only if a vignette exists.
**Simulation:** `R CMD check` and the manifest gate; the
render gate if a report is produced, plus a
seed-determinism check. **Blog:** the render gate above
all, since the deliverable is the site, with `R CMD check`
and the manifest gate applying to any code the posts run.

**Arranging the simulation.** CI runs a reduced pipeline:
the same driver, the same functions, the same seed, with
the replicate count set by a parameter to something small,
perhaps a hundred replicates in place of a hundred
thousand. The full pipeline runs elsewhere, on a cluster,
and its outputs are recorded and deposited.

**What the fixed seed contributes.** It is what makes the
reduced run a genuine reproducibility test rather than a
smoke test. With the seed fixed, the first hundred
replicates of the reduced run are *the same hundred
replicates* the full run begins with, so their summary is
a deterministic value that can be recorded and compared
exactly. Without the seed, the reduced run could only be
checked against a tolerance derived from Monte Carlo
error, which is a much weaker statement and one that
passes even when the generator has changed.

The honest limit: the reduced run verifies that the
machinery reproduces, not that the full study's estimates
are correct, since a hundred replicates estimate the
target quantity poorly. It tests the pipeline, not the
science.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse=true}
## Exercise 6

**The shared role.** Both are an independent re-execution
of the analysis in an environment the author does not
control, performed by a party who has no stake in it
succeeding. A CI runner does this for every committed
change, cheaply and mechanically; a codechecker does it
once for a submitted manuscript, expensively and with
judgment. In both cases the value comes from the same
property: the analysis runs somewhere that carries none of
the author's undeclared state, so anything the author
depended on without knowing it is exposed.

**What a human codechecker catches that the author's own
CI cannot.** The class of failure in which the CI
configuration itself encodes the author's assumptions. CI
is written by the author, so it tests what the author
thought to test, in an environment the author specified,
against outputs the author chose to compare. A workflow
that installs a system library the Dockerfile omits, or
that quietly skips the expensive analysis and checks only
the cheap one, or that compares against a baseline the
author generated after the bug was introduced, passes
indefinitely while the compendium is not reproducible at
all.

A codechecker reads the paper, forms an independent view
of what the analysis is supposed to produce, and checks
that the artifacts produce it. That is a judgment about
whether the right thing was verified, and no amount of
automation supplies it, because the automation is the
thing in question.

The compact statement: CI answers 'does the analysis still
do what it did', and a codechecker answers 'does the
analysis do what the paper says'.
:::

## Further reading

The distinction between capturing reproducibility and
validating it, which organizes this chapter, is drawn out
across the introduction of this book (@sec-intro) and rests
on the general framing of computational reproducibility as
a spectrum in @peng2011.

On independent, external verification, the CODECHECK
initiative described by Nust and Eglen
[@nust2021codecheck] is the most concrete model of
re-execution during peer review, and repays reading for its
account of what a codechecker does and does not certify.
The ACM's artifact review and badging policy [@acm2020]
documents the badge scheme now common at computing venues.

On the persistence of the problem that all this machinery
addresses, Stodden and colleagues [@stodden2018] analyze
the effectiveness of journal reproducibility policies and
find, soberingly, that a policy on paper is not a
reproduction in practice, and Trisovic and colleagues
[@trisovic2022], in re-running thousands of deposited R
files, quantify how often re-execution simply fails, which
is the empirical case for the standing checks this chapter
describes.

For the practices that surround the tooling, the ten simple
rules of Sandve and colleagues [@sandve2013] place
automated checking and independent re-execution among their
recommendations, and connect the mechanics of CI to the
habits that make it worthwhile.
